name: GoPro, Inc.

profile.description: GoPro designs, develops, and markets action cameras, mountable accessories, and subscription services for content creators, athletes, and outdoor enthusiasts. The company's product lineup includes HERO cameras, MAX 360-degree cameras, and the newly launched MISSION 1 Series targeting professional imaging. GoPro has 2.26 million subscribers. Headquartered in San Mateo, California.

innovation.label: WEAK
innovation.analysis: Track Record (1/3): GoPro launched the MISSION 1 Series cameras targeting the professional imaging market in 2026, representing a new market entry beyond its traditional action camera category [1]. However, Q1 2026 revenue declined 26% YoY to $99.1M, camera units sold fell 29% to 313,000, and the company has experienced persistent multi-year revenue contraction from $1.09B in 2022 to a $616M TTM run rate [1][4]. The product refresh is incremental against a backdrop of structural decline. AI Deployment (0/2): GoPro announced an ASUS StoryCube AI content-management partnership and previously discussed an AI content-licensing program with 500,000+ subscriber video hours submitted, but Q1 2026 disclosed no quantified AI revenue or measurable AI-driven savings [1][3]. AI features remain aspirational. Market Share (0/2): GoPro is losing market share rapidly — revenue down 26%, units down 29% YoY — as DJI, Insta360, and AI-enhanced smartphone cameras erode the action camera category from both ends [3]. The brand retains recognition but no longer commands pricing power or share gains. Product Pipeline (1/2): MISSION 1 Series for professional imaging and exploration of defense/aerospace applications represent pipeline diversification, though defense expansion is described as 'exploring opportunities' with no concrete products or timelines [1]. R&D Intensity (0/1): With only 636 employees and declining revenue, absolute R&D investment is minimal relative to peers.

inspiration.label: WEAK
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (2/4): GoPro's original purpose — enabling people to capture and share their most meaningful experiences — was genuine and built a devoted action sports community. However, a decade of strategic missteps (failed Karma drone, abandoned media empire, serial restructurings reducing workforce to 636) has diluted the mission into survival mode [3]. Community Impact (0/2): No evidence of significant charitable programs, foundation activities, or community investment initiatives beyond athlete sponsorships. Employee Retention (0/2): Three rounds of layoffs in 2024 (4%, 15%, then 26%) gutted the workforce from 900+ to 636 [3]. Glassdoor reviews describe CEO Woodman as 'surrounded by yes men,' 'executive leadership VERY disconnected from lower ranks,' and a 'white male bro culture in senior management' [3]. This is an organization in organizational crisis. Insider Buying (0/2): No evidence of meaningful net insider buying. Previous report noted COO and General Counsel selling shares near $0.80. CEO Woodman received stock awards but no open-market purchases identified.

infrastructure.label: WEAK
infrastructure.analysis: Mechanically scored on available metrics. GoPro's financial position has deteriorated sharply — Q1 2026 delivered $99.1M revenue (down 26% YoY) with GAAP gross margin of just 4.3% after a $24.5M component purchase commitment charge and $4.5M inventory loss [1]. Net loss was $80.8M on $99.1M revenue. The balance sheet shows negative stockholders' equity of -$1.9M, $40.7M cash against $72M short-term debt, leaving virtually no financial cushion [1][4]. TTM profit margin of -20.7% and ROE of -236% both score zero mechanically. Revenue growth YoY of -26% is below the -20% floor, also scoring zero. Forward P/E of 14.4 is the sole positive metric, reflecting analyst expectations of a thin profit in FY2026 [4]. Liquidity check passed: 6.7M avg volume x $0.72 = $4.8M daily.

ai_resilience.label: HIGH RISK
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (4/9): GoPro faces meaningful AI disruption on two fronts — AI-enhanced smartphone cameras (Apple computational photography, Samsung Galaxy AI) are closing the image quality gap for the vast majority of use cases that once required a GoPro, and AI-powered editing tools (CapCut, Adobe Firefly) reduce the value of GoPro's Quik software and subscription ecosystem [3]. Chinese competitors DJI and Insta360 integrate AI features at lower prices. GoPro's narrow structural moat — waterproof, shockproof, mountable form factors for extreme conditions — protects the core action sports niche but this represents a shrinking addressable market as casual users migrate to smartphones. AI Opportunity (0/1): Despite announcing an AI content-licensing program and ASUS StoryCube partnership, Q1 2026 disclosed no quantified AI revenue. The GP3 chip's AI NPU has not yet demonstrated measurable revenue contribution [1].

infinite_game.summary: GoPro under Nick Woodman has played a finite game for a decade — chasing trends (drones, media empire, subscription pivot, now pro imaging and defense), executing serial restructurings (three rounds of layoffs in 2024 alone reducing headcount to 636), and repeatedly promising turnaround years that don't materialize. The MISSION 1 launch and defense exploration are the latest in a pattern of reactive pivots driven by survival, not by an enduring Just Cause.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (1/3): GoPro's original cause — enabling people to capture and share their most meaningful experiences — was genuine and created a devoted action sports community [3]. However, the cause has been diluted by a decade of strategic missteps and revenue contraction from $1.09B to $616M TTM. The current strategy pivoting to professional imaging and defense reads as survival rhetoric, not an enduring purpose. Woodman's 21-year tenure shows personal commitment, but the cause no longer drives strategic coherence.

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (0/2): Three rounds of layoffs in 2024 (4%, 15%, 26%) gutted organizational trust, reducing headcount from 900+ to 636 [3]. Glassdoor reviews describe CEO Woodman as 'surrounded by yes men,' with 'executive leadership VERY disconnected from what's happening at the lower ranks' and a 'bro culture in senior management' [3]. Q1 2026's $80.8M net loss on $99.1M revenue with a skeleton crew of 636 employees suggests an organization operating under extreme stress with minimal psychological safety.

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): GoPro's competitive posture has been defensive — protecting brand position against DJI, Insta360, and smartphone cameras rather than learning from their strengths. The company's failure to adapt to Chinese competitors' cost advantages and smartphone AI improvements over a decade suggests a finite competitive mindset focused on what GoPro used to be rather than what it needs to become [3].

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): GoPro has attempted multiple pivots — drones (Karma, failed), media platform (abandoned), subscription services (declining to 2.26M subscribers, down 8% YoY), and now MISSION 1 pro imaging and defense/aerospace exploration [1]. The willingness to try new markets shows some flexibility, but the pattern is reactive pivoting after failure rather than strategic reinvention in service of a Just Cause. Most pivots have underdelivered.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): Woodman's decision to skip the 2025 HERO launch to invest in the GP3 platform and pivot toward professional imaging with MISSION 1 required accepting a year of severe revenue decline [1][2]. Exploring defense/aerospace as a new market is directionally bold. However, after a decade of value destruction from $98 IPO peak to $0.72, these moves are difficult to distinguish from desperation rather than courage. Cutting operating expenses 26% YoY is necessary but painful, not courageous.

investment_thesis: GoPro trades at $0.72 per share ($123M market cap), a sub-$1 stock reflecting near-terminal pessimism about a once-iconic consumer electronics brand. The MISSION 1 Series cameras targeting professional imaging and early-stage defense/aerospace exploration represent attempts to diversify beyond the declining action camera category [1]. Management previously guided FY2026 revenue of $750-$800M (~20% growth) with adjusted EBITDA of $10-$20M, suggesting a path to thin profitability [2]. Operating expenses were cut 26% YoY to $61.6M quarterly, and the 2.26M subscriber base generates recurring revenue of ~$27M/quarter [1]. At 0.20x price-to-sales, if the GP3 chip and MISSION 1 revive demand and gross margins normalize from the Q1 anomaly (4.3% due to one-time charges) back to the historical 30%+ range, significant upside is possible from a low base.
thesis_continued: The bear case is that GoPro is a structurally declining business approaching viability questions. Q1 2026 was catastrophic — revenue fell 26% to $99.1M, camera units dropped 29% to 313,000, gross margin collapsed to 4.3% after $29M in one-time charges, and net loss was $80.8M on $99.1M revenue [1]. The balance sheet shows negative equity of -$1.9M, with only $40.7M cash against $72M short-term debt [1][4]. Subscribers declined 8% YoY to 2.26M, undermining the recurring revenue narrative. Memory price increases are expected to compress gross margins by 500 bps, tariff volatility threatens supply chain, and Chinese competitors DJI and Insta360 continue gaining share with comparable products at lower prices [2][3]. The stock has declined 99% from its $98 IPO peak, and Woodman's leadership over a decade of value destruction — including multiple failed pivots and three rounds of layoffs in 2024 — provides no basis for confidence in execution [3].
key_catalysts: GP3 chip-powered cameras and MISSION 1 Series driving revenue recovery from Q1 2026's $99M trough toward the $750-$800M full-year guidance, with normalized gross margins returning to 30%+
Defense and aerospace market entry providing a higher-margin, less competitive revenue stream that diversifies GoPro beyond consumer electronics
Operating expense discipline at $220-$230M annual run rate enabling breakeven at modest revenue levels, with adjusted EBITDA guidance of $10-$20M for FY2026
key_risks: Balance sheet fragility is approaching existential — $40.7M cash against $72M short-term debt with negative equity of -$1.9M leaves zero margin for error if the GP3/MISSION 1 launches underperform
Structural category decline as AI-enhanced smartphone cameras and Chinese competitors DJI/Insta360 erode GoPro's addressable market — units sold down 29% YoY despite no price increase
Subscriber base declining 8% YoY to 2.26M undermines the recurring revenue thesis and reduces the software/services value that was supposed to offset hardware commoditization
